analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to tell workers when they are being electronically monitored and limits how that data can be used against them.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote in the Senate; after referral it sat in a subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: Employers increasingly use computers, phone taps, and surveillance to track what workers do minute by minute. This bill would have required employers to tell workers in advance exactly what monitoring they use, how often, and how the data will be used; to beep or otherwise signal when monitoring is happening; and to let workers see their own data. It would have banned collecting data on how workers exercise First Amendment rights and stopped employers from using secretly gathered numbers as the sole basis for firing someone or setting quotas, with penalties and lawsuits to enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers whose employers monitor them electronically — call-center operators, telemarketers, data-entry and other tracked staff — plus customers whose calls are secretly observed. They would get advance written notice of surveillance, beeps or lights when monitoring happens, access to the data collected about them, protection for data on their First Amendment activities, and the right to sue with attorney's fees if employers violate the rules. Prospective hires would be told about monitoring before accepting a job.

how_it_helps.text: Employers would have to tell workers in writing, before monitoring begins, what is being watched, how often, and how the data will be used against them.

Workers would gain the right to see all personal data collected about them through electronic monitoring [S3], and employers could not collect data unrelated to job performance [S2], sell or share it [S2], or use it to track how a worker exercises First Amendment rights [S3].

Employers could not use monitoring data as the sole basis for evaluations, discipline, or production quotas unless the worker first got a chance to review it, and could not set quotas purely from secretly gathered statistics.
The bill is enforceable: civil penalties up to $10,000, lawsuits by the Labor Secretary, and private suits with attorney's fees, and workers could not be forced to sign these rights away.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use electronic monitoring, especially call centers, telemarketing firms, and large service operations, would bear compliance costs: written notices, monitoring signals, limits on data use and quotas, and exposure to civil penalties up to $10,000 and private lawsuits. Consumers would not directly pay.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall on employers of all sizes, including small businesses, which would have to issue written notices, install monitoring signals, and police data handling for every monitored worker and customer call.

Private lawsuits with attorney's fees and up to $10,000 civil penalties could generate litigation even where monitoring was disclosed in good faith, and companies could respond by reducing monitoring or moving call-center work abroad.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to workers are real: notice before surveillance, access to their own data, and limits on using secret monitoring stats to fire people or set quotas. The costs to employers are modest compliance burdens — written notices, signal lights, recordkeeping — and possible limits on management flexibility, which is precisely the point. The bill was not well positioned to move, however: it had a single cosponsor, no action in committee, and no sign of negotiation toward a narrower version before the Congress ended.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate, referred to committee and then a subcommittee, and nothing more happened before that Congress ended, so it died without ever reaching the Senate floor.

narrative.text: Senator Paul Simon introduced the Privacy for Consumers and Workers Act on February 22, 1990; the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources.
On March 19, 1990, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employment and Productivity, which took no recorded action on it.
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 with no committee markup, no floor vote, and no further action listed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who electronically monitor their workers — especially call centers and service operations — kept unrestricted ability to surveil employees without notice or consent. Workers gained nothing.

for.name: Paul Simon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its sole sponsor.

for.name: 1 of 55 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: One Senate Democrat cosponsored the bill.

against.name: Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee / Subcommittee on Employment and Productivity
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after the bill was referred on March 19, 1990 — no markup, no report, no vote — so it never reached the Senate floor.

against.name: Business and employer groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandated limits on electronic monitoring of employees during the period the bill was pending.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat with one Democratic cosponsor and never advanced far enough for votes, so no partisan split on the merits shows up in the record.

industries.industry: Telecommunications and other monitored workplaces (call centers, telephone service observation)
industries.note: These employers bore the heaviest compliance burden: written notices, periodic beeps or lights for workers and customers, and legal liability for violations, including for the common practice of secretly listening in on customer service calls. The monitoring itself stays legal; only the secrecy ends.
By requiring notice, access, and limits on how monitoring data can be used for discipline and quotas, the bill would reduce the value of covert, all-encompassing tracking of employees.

Management would lose the ability to use unannounced electronic monitoring data as the sole basis for evaluating, firing, or setting quotas for workers, and would face civil penalties and lawsuits for violations.
